intuition: Sort the numbers so that larger values are to the right. Choose one number, then look for the other two using pointers at opposite ends of the remaining part. If the total is too small, move the left pointer. If it is too large, move the right pointer.

Sorting gives pointer movement a direction. With anchor -1, a total below zero cannot be fixed by decreasing the right value, so only increasing left can help. A positive total requires decreasing right. This argument lets one comparison eliminate many pairs.

Duplicates need separate treatment because a correct zero-sum pair might be followed by identical values at adjacent positions; skipping them preserves completeness while enforcing unique output triplets.

For a fixed first value, a sum below zero rules out every pair using that left value with a smaller right value. A sum above zero similarly rules out that right value with a larger left value. Therefore pointer movements cannot skip a solution. Distinct anchors and duplicate skipping emit each value triplet exactly once.
Sorting uses a copied array; each anchor scans the remaining range once.

concept.question: How can sorted order turn a search for three numbers into a guided pair search?
intuition: Trying every triple repeats many combinations and can report the same values in different orders. Sorting gives us a direction: moving toward larger values increases a sum, while moving toward smaller values decreases it.

Hold one number fixed and balance the remaining pair from opposite ends of the sorted suffix. If the total is below zero, raise its smaller member. If it is above zero, lower its larger member. Equal choices at the same role can be skipped after a solution is recorded.
concept.observation: Use three different positions, and skip equal values at the same choice level to avoid duplicate triplets.
approach: Sort the values and choose one fixed member.
Search the remaining suffix with a low and a high member, moving toward zero.
Record exact matches, skip repeated values, and repeat with the next distinct fixed member.
concept.correctness: For a fixed first member, a sum below zero cannot be repaired by lowering the larger member, so the smaller member may safely advance. A sum above zero similarly requires lowering the larger member. These moves preserve every possible zero-sum pair. Trying each distinct first value covers all triplets; skipping equal role choices removes duplicates without removing distinct value combinations.

complexity.explanation: For each fixed value, the pair search moves across the suffix once. With a linear number of fixed choices, total work is quadratic. A sorted copy uses linear extra memory, plus memory for the returned triplets.

pitfalls: Skip duplicate fixed values and duplicate pairs.
Use different positions even when values are equal.
Keep searching after the first match.
